#9942. ML Modules for Mere Mortals

I think everyone can agree code needs to be modular. Modularity lets us reason locally about our code no matter how big it grows. However, no one seems to agree on how code should be modular. There are a bunch of different approaches and each new language seems to bring their own spin on it.

Today we’re going to talk about a pretty old spin: ML Modules. ML here stands for Meta Language, as seen in SML and OCaml (and not machine learning). Despite SML first appearing in 1983, ML Modules have not caught on. OCaml is the sole production language you’ll find with an ML module system, and at the height of its popularity it’s niche.

This is a shame because ML modules have a lot to offer. We’re going to talk about what ML modules are and then touch a little on why ML modules are. Who better after all to explain modules, than the guy who doesn’t know what’s in a module ?…On second thought, don’t answer that.…I already wrote the blog post.

Modules exist to make our code modular, duh, but what does that mean in practice? I think most programmers have some intuitive sense of modularity:

Most languages have a way to do this, and if they don’t, one gets created for them (looking at you JavaScript).

ML modules achieves this with, you guessed it, the Module. ML modules, however, are a little different from the modules we know and love. To explain their differences, we’ll lean on a made-up Rust-inspired syntax. It will start off looking a little weird and gradually, as we introduce concepts, end up looking really weird (but hopefully more familiar than SML syntax). We’ll start by defining a module with just functions:

AModule bundles together related arithmetic functions as one thing we can reason about. Each function can see every other function in the module. This is useful, but any language with namespaces offers this.

A little more unique is that ML modules will let us put not only function definitions in modules, but also type definitions:

Here we have a Set module with a Set type, which is a sorted Vec. Our module’s functions can refer to the type definitions much the same way they can refer to their module’s function definitions. Okay but that’s not that crazy, still well within the realm of Rust modules.

Not only can modules contain type definitions. Modules themselves have types. A module type is called a signature (so we don’t get it confused with “normal” types). The signature of our Set module is:

A module signature declares every definition of a module alongside its type. This might look similar to the way we define a trait in Rust. That’s because much like traits act as interfaces in Rust, signatures act as interfaces in ML Modules. Modules having signatures is the single most important thing to understand about ML Modules. All the complexity and expressiveness of modules results from them having signatures and the wonderful wacky things that enables.

Signatures resemble the way a C/C++ implementation file conforms to its header. Modules, unlike .cc files, aren’t in a 1:1 relationship with signatures. Our Set module can conform to any signature that it matches. A module matches a signature when it defines every declaration in the signature and they agree on type.

Matching a signature provides Encapsulation , hiding internal details of our module from our public API. Take a look at FullSetSig. Do callers of Set really need to know about index_of? Encapsulation advocates shout a resounding no: index_of is an implementation detail of Set.Set being a Vec and not integral to our Set API.

We can encapsulate index_of by matching our Set module to a new signature:

SetSig removes index_of, hiding the implementation detail. We can then ascribe our signature to our Set module:

Now the rest of our code sees Set as SetSig without index_of. Importantly, our Set module hasn’t changed. index_of is still available inside the module. Ascribing the signature only changes the public view of the module, similar to a private function in Rust.

A module’s definition isn’t the only place we can ascribe a signature. We can also make a “new” module by matching an old module to a new signature. Let’s say we want an InsertOnlySet (never you mind why I need that):

We can create that from our Set module purely by matching the signature:

Now InsertOnlySet is effectively a whole new module, despite the underlying implementation being shared with Set. This is what’s cool about modules. We can repurpose modules “for free” simply by giving them a different signature. If we want to do this in an OO language, we’d have to add a new interface in our class definitiion. But we can slap one of these bad boys anywhere in our codebase.

Ascribing a signature to a module lets us hide implementation details, but there’s a bit of a glaring hole here. Sure we’ve hidden away index_of, but our module broadcasts to the world that type Set is a Vec! Set relies on our vector being kept in sorted order, but anybody is free to write a function:

Nothing but a small flesh wound in our encapsulation. Fortunately, ML modules foresaw this problem and provided a solution using signatures.

Much the same way a signature lets us hide functions, it also lets us hide types. ML Modules call this an abstract type. If we update SetSig to be:

Our signature no longer broadcasts that type Set is Vec. Within the Set module we’re free to use type Set as Vec, but everywhere outside the module type Set is now some unknown type. Because callers know nothing about our newly abstract Set type, all they can do is pass it to and from the methods provided by the Set module. As long as we keep our underlying Vec sorted within Set, we know no one else is able to mess with it. They simply don’t know enough about the type!

Our Set module is nearing perfection, but it still leaves a little to be desired: it only works for i32. Now we could of course write a new module SetU64, SetString, on and on everytime we need one, but c’mon there’s gotta be a better way. This isn’t Go.

Generics is the go-to solution for this problem. Heck we’ve even used it ourselves with Vec. ML Modules, however, have a more modular solution. You can parameterize a module by another a module.

Think of a parameterized module as a function that takes a module and returns another module. To make our Set accept any type and not just i32, we parameterize it by a module that provides the type of our Set’s elements:

Our newly parameterized Set accepts any module that conforms to Elem. Any module can match Elem as long as it has at least a T definition.

With that our Set module supports any type. Except for one teensy detail. I’ve deceived you with some tactical // ...s. If we actually try to implement index_of, we quickly encounter a problem:

We don’t know how to compare T’s. Rust’s Ord would solve this, of course, but ML modules have modules not traits. Set doesn’t take in just a type, however, it takes in a full module. If we need to know how to compare T’s, we can just ask our Elem module:

Now it’s clear how to implement index_of:

With our parameterized module implemented, we can create new Set modules by applying them to new argument modules:

SetU32.Set is a Vec and provides an interface that takes and returns u32 instead of i32. We can do it again as easy as:

Just like that, a whole new module. This time a set of Strings. I could do this all day.

Because we accept a module, we can request anything a module can hold (even a whole other submodule or parameterized module!). The downside is that we have to specify the whole module every time. We have to specify cmp every time we apply our Set module. Rust traits let us write Ord for a type once and use it everywhere implicitly.

In practice, we don’t actually repeat how to order our type every time we want a Set. Recall that a signature will match any module that provides what it needs. If we make a big module called U64:

Then we can use that as our argument to Set:

But hang on, we got into this whole Module business to break up our code. Now we’ve got to dump everything into one module just in case we need it later? That’s not very cash modular of us.

ML modules have a final feature to get us the best of both worlds: include. include expands a module inline within another module. We’re free to split up our U64 module into various submodules: U64Order, U64Arithmetic, etc. Our final U64 module only has to include these submodules:

Modules can be organized into logical components and then combined later to provide convenience (wow!). We’re free to cut up and reassemble modules at the whims’ of the wind. We can even apply a module and include it inline:

Why do you need one module that’s a bunch of overlapping Sets? I don’t know! I’m not your supervisor. Either way, modules will happily let you do it.

We’ve covered the basics of modules. Let’s take a look at a more involved examples to get a sense of what modules can offer. We’re gonna use modules to assemble a little build executor. Out build step will be a parameterized module:

Where CacheSig represents a cache of build steps and RunnerSig represents running some command:

For brevity we’ll keep these pretty simple, but hopefully you can imagine how these might expand. We can then implement BuildSet in terms of our input modules:

Our build functions takes a list of source files, compiles them, and then links the object files into a final binary. How does run tell when it’s compiling and when it’s linking? Don’t worry about it! Now that we’ve set that up we can toggle the functionality of our build by controlling what modules we pass to BuildStep. For a real build, we’ll want something like an in-memory cache:

Next we’ll want something that runs our commands:

We can then assemble our build system via:

But maybe we don’t always want caching. Maybe we want a build that always reruns actions for local testing. We simply swap out our cache module:

Our build system works first try. We wouldn’t write the code bad, of course, but just in case we might want to test it. A FakeRunner will let us do just that:

Because FakeRunner is a parameterize module, we can create a new module (and a new empty COMMANDS) every time we apply it:

If we want to check that caching works we can extend our tests with a new fake runner and compare their commands:

This isn’t earth shattering stuff. If we wanted to replicate this setup in an OO language, however, we would need runtime objects or, heaven forbid, a DI framework. Here we can do it all by wiring up modules statically.

Hopefully this has helped you see what’s cool about modules. Module’s power lies in their signatures. What would require a newtype wrapper or a visibility change in other languages can be accomplished by simply changing the signature a module is viewed at.

With abstract types, this allows for constructing webs of encapsulation where each piece knows precisely what it needs to about its neighbor and no more. Signatures act as this encapsulation boundary, freeing us to reason about our code modularly. As long as our module conforms to the expected signature we can contort and refactor it to our wildest whims and trust that it will continue to integrate into our system as expected. ML Modules are neat and I think they deserve more love and exploration in programming languages.

In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

In September, we experienced two incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.

In August, we experienced five incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.

#9940. Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

Update: Inkling 2 Small is here! 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family. We have updated this post with a new section on Inkling 2 Small, covering what changed in the architecture and how to run it with transformers.

Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:

In this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it. The rest of the post covers inference, use cases, post-training, and deployment, with examples built on the first-generation checkpoints.

Inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text. It is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered (pun intended) with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a new wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

Inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

Short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

MoE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

The multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

Inkling 2 is the next generation of the family. It takes text and image inputs (but no audio), and generates text. It keeps the core ideas of Inkling's decoder:

Almost everything around that core was redesigned, though. The layers read from the residual stream differently, attention is bounded and gated, the MoE is simpler and wider, and the vision tower is now a real vision transformer.

Let's go over the most notable changes together:

Block attention residuals: In a standard transformer, every layer adds its output to the residual stream, and the next layer reads it. Inkling 2 has no single residual stream. Instead, it groups its 48 layers into 8 blocks of 6 and keeps one sum per block:

A sublayer (attention or MLP) doesn't read one of these sums directly. It attends over depth, which means at each token position, it treats the finished block summaries plus the current partial block as a short sequence, and takes a softmax-weighted mix of them.

The query is a single learned vector per sublayer. The keys and values are the RMS-normalized block summaries at that position. So the weights differ from token to token, depending on what each block wrote there.

In other words, each sublayer learns how much to draw from each earlier stage of the network, rather than always reading the sum of everything. By the last layer, there are up to 9 sources to choose from (the embeddings, 7 finished blocks and the current partial block), and the final norm reads its input the same way. Global attention layers learn three queries, so their query, key and value projections can each draw on a different mix of blocks.

Dynamic short convolutions: The short convolutions on keys and values in the global attention layers are now dynamic. The 4 taps of each convolution are a fixed learned weight plus a per-token weight predicted from the input, shared within each key/value head. So the model can change, token by token, how much local context goes into each key and value. All short convolutions also rescale their residual sum to keep its variance stable through depth.

A leaner, wider MoE: Each layer has 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, and the shared experts are gone.

A new vision encoder: Inkling encoded images with a lightweight hierarchical MLP. Inkling 2 uses a 23-layer vision transformer based on the Perception Encoder. It has the following properties:

Several images are packed into one sequence, and each image only attends to itself.

Inkling 2 uses the same Auto classes as Inkling. Make sure to have updated transformers to run the model.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

This model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

The easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

For multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

Inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

In practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

You can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

Using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

You can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

This starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

Llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

Pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

We have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

We have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

If you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

We post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

If you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

To deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/new/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching)

Once the endpoint is up, you can query as follows.

Releasing a natively multimodal model (text, vision, and audio) open-weights is a huge step forward for the open-source AI ecosystem! Having variable and controllable thinking effort built into a MoE architecture makes Inkling a really attractive foundation for fine-tuning. Excited to test out the smaller 12B active parameter variant for local agent workflows at https://geometrydashsubzero.io

#9939. Microsoft struggling to fix massive cloud outage that's taken down email and Intune

‘Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief’

Microsoft is struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became “overwhelmed” and its attempts to fix the problem failed.

The incident started at around 18:00 UTC on November 12, and meant services including Exchange Online, Teams, Copilot 365, and Defender for Office 365 became unavailable. Admins trying to figure out what was wrong couldn’t access tools like Intune or the Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center – they went down, too.

On its X feed, Microsoft blamed “a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

The company said it hasn’t spotted any changes to its systems that might have sparked the incident, but its early investigation “indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”

The company’s status page offers contradictory information, saying Microsoft’s people are “assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery.”

According to a Xeet published at around 22:00 UTC, Microsoft said it found and validated an alternative service health check method, “which allowed a subset of affected servers to successfully return to service.”

“We're continuing to work through restarting and validating the affected servers to safely return them to service, and we're exploring opportunities to expedite this process,” the company wrote.

“We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the status page advises. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.”

The incident means email is not flowing for many Microsoft customers: friends and family of Reg writers tell us their working days are severely disrupted.

Microsoft’s most recent Xeet on the matter, published about an hour before this story went live, says it's trying to validate a potential recovery by “isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.”

But the software giant hasn’t offered any timeline for full service restoration.

This is a developing situation and The Reg will update this story as more information becomes available. ®

UPDATED AT 00:35 UTC November 13 to add news that Microsoft says it has brought some servers back online and that they "initially remain healthy" but "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic."

"We're analyzing diagnostic data from these servers with our networking and platform experts to determine what's triggering this behavior," the company advised.

#9937. DOJ takes aim at $1.2B in Binance loot as FBI disrupts North Korean scam

‘FaceStealer’ scam tied to $400M+ theft, 900+ webcam recordings

The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft.

The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months.

It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks.

The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers.

First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible.

“You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles.

“They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday.

The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite.

Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told.

“When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.”

The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix.

Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam.

The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet, which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff.

“The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.”

The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group.

Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “sophisticated, multi-stage campaign” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.”

Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department's court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®

#9936. Beating the frontier on NetHack

November 13, 2026 | Paul Ryan, Member of Technical Staff | Mikail Khan, Research intern | Will Wilson, Co-founder and CEO

Monthly reliability and distributed systems news, curated for teams building critical software.

Please enable JavaScript in your browser to load and submit this form.

Check your inbox for your confirmation message.

We couldnât submit your form. Please try again later.

Thatâs not quite true for computer game history (though NetHack was very early and very influential), but itâs true for the history of Antithesis. The company started when I got lunch with Dave and said: âletâs make the FDB simulator but for everythingâ and he was like: âno, letâs make a fuzzer so smart it can beat NetHack,â and then we gradually realized that we were actually talking about the same thing.

In the years that followed, NetHack continued to inspire and challenge us. The first Antithesis VCS repo (long since deleted) was called âfuzzhackâ because it was a fuzzer for NetHack. Before we built our deterministic hypervisor, we tried Hermit-style deterministic Linux userland because itâs the bare minimum you need to beat NetHack. NetHack inspired our thinking about the importance of strategy, about the importance of code coverage and also about its inadequacy, and about why you need intrinsic curiosity rewards to have any hope of applying AI to this problem. NetHack inspired many of our early experiments in visualization. Wanting to interactively explore NetHack performance and coverage maps is why we wrote the first version of the reactive notebook that now powers our UI. Processing reams of NetHack data that wouldnât fit in memory was why we decided to put a GCP subscription on my credit card so we could crunch the data in BigQuery, which later led us to invent skip trees, and finally Pangolin.

All of this is because it was a worthy adversary â perhaps even what my colleague David MacIver likes to call a âdragon problem.â NetHack is famously difficult for human beings because it combines permadeath, extreme information scarcity (reading the source code of the game to figure out how to beat it is practically a rite of passage for aficionados), and a brutal intolerance for error. But itâs also very difficult for autonomous systems like fuzzers and AI agents due to its sprawling state space and to the need for long-horizon planning to make any real progress. People have written bots that have successfully beaten the game, but despite Metaâs investment in the NetHack Learning Environment, AI agents have struggled with it. The wins that both the hardcoded bots and the AIs (most recently GPT-6 Astra) have eked out have been skin-of-their-teeth affairs involving lucky seeds and âbeginner-friendlyâ roles. Nobody has produced a system that can reliably and quickly beat the game over and over again as any character build.

âBeginner-friendlyâ by NetHack standards, at least.

Antithesis can now find a path to victory within 5 wall-clock minutes on nearly 80% of NetHack seeds. Moreover, the median time to victory within the seeds that finish is under 2 minutes. To explain how we did this, we need to let you in on a secret: Antithesis is not just a system for unopinionated state space exploration, it is also something akin to a probabilistic programming language, a new computing paradigm for partially describing tests or other tasks and letting search and optimization fill in the rest. When you put this tool in the hands of capable AI agents, they can do things like beat NetHack in 30 seconds. But firstâ¦ back to our story.

The game is considered one of the hardest games in the world, with winning episodes lasting hundreds of thousands of steps, and a permadeath setting that starts agents at the beginning in a whole new world if they die in the dungeon. â Insights from the NeurIPS 2021 NetHack Challenge, Hambro et al.

The overall goal of NetHack is straightforward to state, if not to achieve. You begin on the top floor of a dungeon; your objective, the Amulet of Yendor, is at the bottom, in Molochâs Sanctum. To beat the game, you must descend to Sanctum, take the Amulet from the High Priest of Moloch, and make your way back to the top. Upon exiting the dungeon with the Amulet in your possession, you are transported to the Elemental Planes; from here, you must travel to the Astral Plane, seek out the high altar of your god, and offer the Amulet there, for which your god will grant you immortality and ascension to demigodhood. (Beating the game is called ascending.)

When I started working on fuzzing NetHack in 2020, there was minimal prior art. We were a new company, building new tools and learning in real time how best to hold them, and previous bot ascensions were few. Two, to be precise, both targeting an earlier version of the game.

SWAGGINZZZ, an RNG-predicting bot, had speed-ascended a Tourist in 2019 using zero-turn RNG manipulations that were quickly patched out. (This remains the fastest ascension on NAO, a popular NetHack server, in both real time and turn count.)

BotHack, an earlier (2015) hand-rolled expert system made of about 16,000 lines of Clojure, had ascended a Valkyrie (the easiest role in NetHack and standard beginner recommendation, with strong melee and intrinsic cold resistance and stealth), and later a Samurai and a Knight, using a technique known as pudding farming.

In NetHack, thereâs a monster called a black pudding, which can divide when hit with iron weapons. When BotHack was written, a black pudding could leave a corpse when slain, which could produce a death drop: a random item on the corpse square that the monster didnât have while alive â any item, from the weak orcish dagger to the coveted amulet of life saving. Consequently, a player who could hit black puddings for minimal damage could divide and kill them indefinitely, producing effectively unbounded black pudding corpses (which could be sacrificed at an altar to gain favor with the playerâs god) and effectively unbounded random items. A player willing to grind through thousands of turns of pudding farming could generate as many amulets of life saving as they wanted.

BotHack didnât sacrifice puddings at altars â its game plan didnât need to â but it relied on pudding farming for experience and items. A player must reach experience level (XL) 14 to become worthy of the Quest, whose completion is required to beat the game; BotHackâs fifty thousand turns of pudding farming took it from XL 11 to XL 22. It assembled much of its ascension kit (a shopping list of items that experienced players will collect before entering the late game) from pudding farming: a full kit of armor, an assortment of scrolls and magical rings, a pair of gauntlets of power â and a Hawaiian shirt, which provides no value by itself but can be enchanted to +7.

In the subsequent version of NetHack, 3.6.0, pudding farming was removed.

Will and Dave had started with 3.6.0, all the way back in 2017. We didnât want to downgrade. So pudding farming was out.

â NetHack played by our agent, internal Zulip, April 2020

We began with a simple agent that fed random bytes to NetHack and looked for new code coverage, a notebook to display coverage maps, and some functionality to play back recordings of our agentâs runs. We kicked off a run and quickly found a problem: after about an hour, we stopped making progress. 47 cores of our 48-core machine sat idle, and the remaining coreâs CPU was locked at 100% utilization, returning zero new states.

We were relieved to find that we could deterministically reproduce the bug. After investigating, we found a minimal repro: start a new game, type ;|:, and, as Will put it, ânow your computer is a space heater.â Locally, a player could ^C out of the pathological state, but NetHackâs input loop itself had ceased to respond, and our agent could no longer reach the game. We opened GDB, read the function at the bottom of the backtrace, and found a comment: /* warning: no bounds checking performed */.

These were the early days; this wasnât yet a given.

We patched a workaround into our harness and tried again. In this run, our agent gained its first-ever experience level and found dungeon level 2 for the first time! And then we had a different problem.

Dungeon levels in NetHack are lazily generated. A level is only created when the player reaches it for the first time. In normal play, NetHack presents the appearance of a pre-existing dungeon, but in our tree fuzzing context, there are many level 2s that can be reached. From the same stairwell on level 1, an agent could descend immediately to level 2a, or wait a turn, burning some RNG values, and descend to a different level 2bâ¦ or wait two turns, and so on. From any level 2, thereâs a lot of work to do to reach level 3 â but how could an agent with so many options commit to one?

We also had more prosaic problems. Our agent generated random bytes to use as input. Most random bytes arenât sensible inputs, and donât make progress; worse, some inputs lead to menus that are hard to exit. Every time the fuzzer sent a V, it had to advance through a 14-page description of NetHackâs history, in a menu where most possible inputs donât advance. Our agent spent a lot of time reading.

I had heard that NetHack was complex, but this didnât really sink in until I played the game past a certain point. â Mikael Henaff, First NetHack ascension, and insights into the AI capabilities it requires

> is there some kind of kill count we could use to train the Antithesis wizard to kill

This is one of the weirder work-related discussions Iâve ever seen. â Justin Moore, internal Zulip, February 2024

With little progress to show and much foundational work to be done, our energies drifted from NetHack to more tractable games. Each one taught us a valuable lesson.

From Super Mario Bros., we learned the effectiveness of maximizing a single progress metric; defining this metric would later prove to be key to progress in NetHack. From The Legend of Zelda and Metroid, we learned to work with the complex state spaces of adventure games: to deliberately linearize the many possible orders down to one concrete game plan, and to manage inventories of consumable resources. From Castlevania, we learned the importance of pruning doomed states; we expanded this into a definition of just how doomed a state was. How beset was our hero by monsters? How incomplete was our agentâs inventory? How much HP was it missing? And from Tetris, we learned the usefulness of custom input generatorsâ¦ and that sometimes our value functions have bugs.

At this point, itâs worth thinking about the shape of NetHackâs state space. We had understood the importance of this question since the beginning, but it was particularly underscored by Gradius. After we beat Gradius with the style of config weâd refined over time â defining a value function, building an inventory, pruning doomed states, and making progress through levels â we realized it could also be beaten by a strategy that only pruned doomed states. The whole game is an autoscroller! Every state that isnât doomed leads inexorably to a better one, so depth is all you need.

NetHackâs state space is very different: both extremely deep and extremely broad. One adventurer could find a wand of wishing on dungeon level 2 and get most of an ascension kit in the early game; another could step on an unlucky polymorph trap and be turned into a quivering blob, or be zapped by the proverbial (but possible) Gnome with the Wand of Death. Quaffing from a fountain could grant the player a wish, but could also summon an angry water demon â or, worse, a horde of venomous snakes. And unlike Gradius, with its linear progression through the seven stages, NetHackâs game plan is highly nonlinear and almost fractally complex.

What about depth? As weâve said, the high-level objective is to retrieve the Amulet of Yendor from Molochâs Sanctum and sacrifice it on the correct high altar on the Astral Plane. To reach Molochâs Sanctum, the player must complete the Invocation Ritual, which is as follows: while standing on a certain square on the bottom floor of Gehennom, light seven candles on the Candelabrum of Invocation, ring the Bell of Opening, and read from the Book of the Dead. Upon completion, a ring of fire and a moat will surround the invoker, and the downstair to the Sanctum will be revealed.

To complete the Invocation Ritual, the player must first find the three items it requires. The Candelabrum of Invocation is guarded by Vlad the Impaler, whose tower must be found; the Bell of Opening is in the possession of the playerâs quest nemesis, who lives beyond a magic portal to be found somewhere in the Dungeons of Doom; and the Book of the Dead is in the possession of the Wizard of Yendor himself, who, after being killed for the first time, will revive himself to harass the player for the rest of the game.

To be admitted to the Quest, the player must be judged worthy by its Leader; to defeat the nemesis, the player must be skilled in both offense and defense, and be well on the way to the ascension kit.

The Quest is often the first required branch that players tackle, after taking on the Gnomish Mines and retrieving a good item from the optional Sokoban levels, but it can be done at any point before the invocation ritual â it may be unwise to slay the Wizard of Yendor before thinking about the Quest, but the game wonât stop you.

A long time passed. Our NES scorecard grew. The NeurIPS NetHack Challenge came and went. NetHack 3.6.7 was released, and we upgraded from 3.6.0, but we were an early-stage startup with many irons in the fire, and ascending fell off our to-do list.

âWe told our Nethack AI to level up, and it abused the RNG and a cursed ring of polymorph to optimize only that one thingâ could be a fun blog post in itself. â Will, internal Zulip, February 2024

In 2024, we felt ready to attack NetHack again, and kicked off some new runs. One of these runs smashed our old record, reaching the twelfth floor of the dungeons at experience level 22. (The playerâs experience level, or XL, starts at 1 and caps at 30.) With no weapon, no armor, and mediocre stats, this run â a human wizard â was not on the path to ascension, but it was a new milestone. Curious about how this happened, we opened the best moment in our multiverse debugger â and found, welded to our human wizardâs foreclaw, a cursed ring of polymorph. Antithesis the Necromancer had come down with polymorphitis!

This run had just been lucky, but it gave us some ideas.

Polymorph is one of NetHackâs more complex mechanics. With a certain form of magic, anything can be turned into anything else of its type: a lucky zap of a wand of polymorph can turn a fedora into a pair of speed boots, or a black dragon into a woodchuck, but an unlucky step on a polymorph trap could turn the player into a newt. The danger of an uncontrolled self-polymorph leads most players to seek out polymorph control, which removes the element of randomness and allows them to specify which monster theyâd like to become. Our agent didnât have this, but our tree fuzzing model meant it didnât need it.

Polymorphitis helped us in two different ways. First, turning into a monster could provide us with useful capabilities: some monsters can fly, some can walk through walls, and some have very powerful attacks, and a player who takes the form of that monster inherits its abilities. Second, an uncontrolled polymorph has a chance to cause own-race polymorph: a human, for instance, might simply turn into a human, or a gnome into a gnome. Own-race polymorph, in addition to having a 1-in-10 chance to change the playerâs gender, applies random deltas to experience level and stats, in ways designed to have an expected value of zero. Our fuzzer can make great use of an expected value of zero. Since weâd configured our fuzzer to care about experience gained, every favorable own-race polymorph in this run was saved as an interesting state to explore further from, and the fuzzer was able to ride the expected value of zero from XL 1 to XL 22.

In a follow-up run, we found that uncontrolled polymorphitis could reliably get us to the highest experience level possible. There were unlucky polymorphs along the way, which the fuzzer didnât prune â not all monsters can wear armor, or even hold a weapon, so we reached XL 30 with minimal inventory â but with the ability to become a fearsome jabberwock in our pocket, we werenât convinced this mattered.

Jabberwocks have good natural armor, decent magic resistance, and four 2d10 attacks per turn. Theyâre vulnerable to immediate beheading by the Vorpal Blade, but this is a rare artifact weapon whose generation the fuzzer can easily prevent. We never saw one.

We told our fuzzer to seek out polymorphitis on purpose. The next night, after retrieving the luckstone at the end of the Gnomish Mines, it reached the Castle â dungeon level 27, one floor before the Valley of the Dead which heralds the entrance to Gehennom. The run after that unlocked the Quest.

The Quest state, alas, looked doomed. With no weapons and no armor, we were no match for the ravens of the Lonely Tower, let alone the Dark One, and the downstair to the next Quest level was far away. The portal back to the dungeon was blocked by a crocodile and a battalion of elves, so we couldnât retrieve the resources weâd lost when weâd absentmindedly turned into an ant. And our magical power was spent. Without armor, we couldnât advance; without weapons, we couldnât retreat. Our only choice, it seemed, was between being pecked to death in the search for the upstair and being slaughtered by the elves, one of whom had a wand of fire. The only thing in our inventory was our cursed ring of polymorph.

This seemed like an interesting challenge, so we loaded the state in our multiverse debugger and kicked off an exploration campaign, and our agent surprised us all by finding a way through: it turned into a purple worm and ate all the monsters. The next problem was much more tractable: we needed to talk to Neferet the Green in the Lonely Towerâs throne room to receive the quest, but our purple worm, being a worm and thus without hands, couldnât open the door. This too was resolved by polymorph.

With proof of progress in hand, we started thinking about defining a value function. Weâd gotten this far with simple placeholders â experience, dungeon level, score, code coverage, and enough nutrition not to starve â but we knew weâd soon need to give the fuzzer a real game plan. Our next run made it to the Castleâ¦ but its best state was doomed.

In this screenshot, our character is the h: Antithesis the Master Mind Flayer, formerly a wizard. Around us is a one-tile passage, blocked on our right by a cockatrice: one of the most feared monsters in all of NetHack, standing on the upstair. Not only can the cockatriceâs hiss turn you to stone, a delayed instadeath with only a few methods of prevention, any skin contact with a cockatrice will immediately turn you to stone. The master mind flayerâs primary attack is to suck the brains of its foe with its tentacles â skin contact! If we attack to the right, we immediately die; if we donât attack, we die a slow death.

With more fuzzing, we could have found a convenient polymorph or a more favorable Castle, but this was only a test run: the instrumentation by which the fuzzer read information out of the game was still under active development, and because weâd patched the instrumentation directly into NetHack in a lazy way, every change required a new run. We started over and iterated, and in time, we found the Quest.

Our fuzzer keeps a distribution of interesting states to explore further from, rather than only ever exploring from a single frontier. This stuck-at-the-Castle scenario is one reason why. Our value function can only imperfectly approximate the true value function, so it has to degrade gracefully when itâs wrong â in this case, by exploring from the dungeon level above and going down to the Castle with a different RNG value, producing a different Castle. Even if our strategies had only ever advised states on this lineage of the Castle, though, there are a few ways we couldâve gotten out. When a state is advised, the fuzzer can choose to rewind it slightly and roll out from its recent ancestor, which couldâve put us on the floor above. And if all else fails, we couldâve tried to stay alive long enough to roll a new polymorph form.

It was around this time that we switched our characterâs role from Wizard to Valkyrie. The Valkyrie has a powerful starting kit, strong combat abilities, and a melee-focused playstyle that we thought would be much easier for our fuzzer to navigate than the Wizardâs menu-heavy spellcasting.

we should write the blog post now just to title it âWe made it to hell!â â Harrison Brown, internal Zulip, May 2024

With our agentâs tree fuzzing powers, we could make use of polymorphitis in ways no human could. This was what drove us to the Quest. But our system had another power, which we used to scout the next phases of the game: the ability to alternate between fuzzing campaigns and linear campaigns, sequences of input manually specified by a human. (We planned to eliminate human input in time, and eventually we did, but in the early days it gave us the useful ability to scout multiple bottlenecks at once.) The fuzzer could get to the Quest home level, but could it reach the Norn to receive the Quest? After reaching the Norn, could it make its way to the fortress of Lord Surtur, the Valkyrieâs quest nemesis? After reaching the fortress, could it defeat Lord Surtur? And after defeating Lord Surtur, could it retrieve the Bell of Opening from his corpse?

Instead of solving one problem only to be faced by another, we could face them all in parallel. We fuzzed to Quest Home and then branched: one campaign would fuzz, to see what the fuzzer could do alone, and another could send NetHack a series of human-generated inputs to solve the current problem and progress to the next. We got into a rhythm: kick off a job overnight, analyze it in the morning, tune the config in response after lunch, and kick off a new job seeded with the last runâs best state at the end of the day. In time, we made it past the Castle (by turning into a jabberwock to fly over the moat) to the Valley of the Dead.

From here, the game was open. We were out of the early gameâs scramble for resources and well into the midgame. We had options. What to do? We could go back for that luckstone at Minesâ End. We could defeat Croesus at Fort Ludios for gold beyond our wildest dreams. We could wander the dungeons in search of loot. But, most importantly, we could traverse the Castle â and here we had a decision to make.

In a corner of the Castle, there lies a special treasure chest. Inside this chest is a wand of wishing, which is the most powerful item in the game. Zap the wand of wishing and type in the name of an item, and that item is yours. But while our fuzzerâs input generation had grown more sophisticated than the random bytes of early years, randomly generating the exact sequence blessed rustproof +3 gray dragon scale mail was far beyond its abilities. With linear campaigns, a human could make use of the wand, but with uncontrolled polymorphitis, armor was out of the question, and weapons would likely be lost. What to do? We considered wishing for highly enchanted rings and polymorphing into a monster that could eat rings to gain their powers, but in the end, given the fuzzerâs sharp division of responsibility between tactics and strategy and our commitment to eventually getting a fully autonomous run, we resolved to let the wand go.

With a few exceptions. You canât wish for the three invocation items, your own roleâs quest artifact, the Amulet of Yendor, or a source of more wishes, and wishes for artifacts have a chance to fail depending on how many artifacts have been generated.

Or so I thought. The building blocks that we later used to unlock wishing had been there all along.

We traveled through Gehennom to Vladâs Tower, home of Vlad the Impaler and the Candelabrum of Invocation â and then realized our instrumentation was once again insufficient. We thought we were unlikely to beat Vlad the Impaler without a value function to guide us, but our value function had no way to know that Vlad was there. We would have to add more code to our harness to tell the fuzzer about Vlad â and since our harness was patched into NetHack itself and many changes to it modified NetHackâs internal data structures, we knew weâd soon have to restart.

We could have written some linear campaigns to beat Vlad by hand, but in the end, the decision to restart was made for us. Weâd been advancing slowly over the course of weeks, starting each nightâs run from the best game state found by the previous nightâs run, constructing a chain of runs whose beginning â and build artifacts â receded further every day into the past. Eventually the build artifacts aged out of what our retention policy allowed and were deleted. Lesson learned! We switched to a setup with a longer retention period and kicked off a new run from scratch.

âmy variable named _totally_safe_buffer has people asking a lot of questions already answered by the variable nameâ â Harrison Brown, internal Zulip, September 2025

âMan I hate C.â â Will, internal Zulip, September 2025

Our plan was to beat NetHack, but our fuzzer is a tool for finding bugs, and find bugs it did. In our next run, we saw an interesting termination:

We opened the multiverse debugger again and investigated. At the moment before the double free, we were engulfed by a purple worm â and punished, a niche mechanic in NetHack with whole source files to support it.

There are only two ways for a character to become punished: by reading a scroll of punishment, which is almost always a bad idea, or as a consequence of prayer to an extremely angry god. A punished character is attached to a heavy iron ball (the only item of the âiron ballâ object class) by a heavy iron chain (the only item of the âchainâ object class). The ball and chain drag behind the player, are rendered on screen, and have many unique effects; for our purposes here, it suffices to note that a punished player may pick up the heavy iron ball and add it to inventory, and that the game has special logic to track the state of the ball and handle the rendering of it and the chain.

We still had code coverage as a component of our value function. The fuzzer, seeking to visit as much of the code as it can, had found a way to become punished, then become engulfed by a purple worm, then pick up the ball, then save â which triggered a double free! For a minute, we were excited, thinking weâd found an unknown bug â but then we found that a development version had already patched it out. The DevTeam thinks of everything.

Or do they? We later found a different bug that, as far as I know, was unreported at the time. Certain artifacts, at certain times, can blast the player for damage, and a polymorphed player who takes fatal damage will revert to base form rather than die. While polymorphing into a yellow light, the Orb of Fate blasted us, which depleted the lightâs meager HP and produced an assertion failure reading del_light_source: not found.

Alas, I was busy and didnât file a ticket. I posted it on our internal Zulip on Oct 1, 2025. It was filed almost a year later as issue #1682.

We didnât investigate this very much, because it led us to a more severe problem: from the moment that found the assertion failure to the frontier of our exploration, our alignment with our god had dropped to -70. This explained why the Orb â our roleâs own artifact! â blasted us, but it looked like a horrible bug in our strategy. The light source bug was a curiosity, but failure to maintain alignment threatened to impede our progress â there were the consequences of negative alignment themselves to worry about, but also, if it could get this wrong, what else could it be getting wrong? But it was just a NetHack moment. On the variant of the Medusa level whose entrance contains a puddle of water, a magic trap, and a gremlin, we stepped on the magic trap, which tamed all adjacent monsters. If a gremlin comes into contact with water, it spawns an additional gremlin. One accidentally tamed gremlin, locked in a room with a puddle, became a roomful of them; our fuzzer hacked its way through the horde to escape and incurred a -15 alignment penalty per kill.

We also found a few known issues, a minor bug in our instrumentation (revisiting a level on which an item with a custom name had been dropped would crash the game), and one especially literal bug: in one run, our inventory contained a potion that was also a giant ant corpse.

Every item in inventory has an int corpsenm. For most items, this is set to -1; for corpses, itâs set to the index of a monster class, to track which type of corpse it is. This particular potion had a corpsenm of 0: the ID of the giant ant.

With further refinement of our strategy, we were able to beat the Quest and descend to Gehennom without manual interventionâ¦ and then we hit the really bad bug. Try as it might, the fuzzer couldnât pass the tenth floor of Gehennom. Every time it tried, NetHack would segfault.

The situation was otherwise promising. Weâd eliminated every point of manual intervention. We knew we could beat Vlad the Impaler. Weâd need a plan to obtain the seven candles for the Candelabrum, but in the worst case we could backtrack all the way to the Gnomish Mines, near the beginning of the game. If we could just fix the segfault, we could probably ascend by the end of the year.

In retrospect, our problems were likely overdetermined. We had an unusual setup for launching the game that weâd last thought about in 2020. Our harness directed all input to NetHack itself and died alongside it, so we couldnât run diagnostics on the rest of the system. Our initial investigations pointed to string fortification in the Nix compiler wrappers, which had bitten us in other ways some years ago, and to a part of the NetHack codebase with a long and storied history of memory safety bugfixes.

We fixed our harness, we turned off source fortification, and we pored over sp_lev.c, but no matter what we did, every run hit a wall: past a certain point, progress was impossible, and every descent ended in a crash. We couldnât even tell which level the game crashed trying to generate, since we had no way of reaching it, and teleporting to the level in NetHackâs debug mode made the segfaults disappear. We became unsure if weâd even succeeded in disabling source fortification. The only hint we had to go on was the discovery, late in the search, that the crash couldnât happen until weâd seen the Valley of the Dead. Over time, the effort lost steam: weâd kick off a run from time to time to see if anything new could be learned, but after we missed our 2024 target, the enthusiasm was gone.

Then, in late 2025, a particularly unlucky run segfaulted while entering the Valley of the Dead, with a slightly different message. With another year of diagnosing bugs for customers under our belt, and another year of tricks up our sleeve, we were finally able to get a diagnosticâ¦

The buffer, located in the part of our instrumentation code that told our agent about the levelâs monsters, was not totally safe. We made it ten times larger and the segfaults went away.

Welcome back to experience level 28. You totally digest it. â NetHack

Our next run got off to a good start. After the fuzzer spent the early game bashing monsters with a suit of bronze plate mail, it found the ring of polymorph (and the similarly useful ring of teleportation), beat the Quest, and descended past the Castle to Gehennom. We still didnât have a strategy in place for the Vlad the Impaler fight, but we were confident that our days of starting over to fix the harness were behind us: weâd had plenty of time to improve the instrumentation over the course of our many restarts, the remaining issues could be solved in strategy alone, and weâd much improved our insight into the game.
