#9933. Alibaba's Qwen3.8 re-educated with a more Western worldview

Open weight model can now say things Chinese authorities don't like

An American AI lab has re-educated Qwen3.8-27B, a popular open-weight large language model from Alibaba, so the software forgets its Chinese ancestry.

Nous Research, an Austin, Texas-based AI lab, has subjected the model to re-education through training, not to be confused with China's "Re-education Through Labor" system.

With the help of a post-training process, Qwen3.8-27B has been reborn under the name Arete "to reinforce Western values on a Chinese-trained model."

What qualifies as a "Western value" remains open to interpretation.

"Open-weight Chinese models are among the strongest available, but they ship with state-aligned behavior baked into the weights," Nous Research wrote in a blog post.

Your correspondent tested this with a variant model, Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-6bit, locally. Asked about events during 1989 in Tiananmen Square, the model either refused to discuss the topic or provided euphemistic response. What's perhaps more surprising is that Anthropic claims operators affiliated with Alibaba's Qwen lab used outputs from its Claude models to train competing AI models via distillation.

Nous Research, maker of the Hermes Agent, cites that sort of censorship as a risk for users of AI models trained in China. The concern comes amid broader scrutiny of Chinese influence in the tech industry, heightened by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation following controversy involving a woman US intelligence has accused of spying for China.

Nous says the risk posed by Chinese-made AI models go beyond promoting Beijing's worldview. Some Middle Kingdom models have been found to produce more vulnerable code under certain conditions, according to a study by Booz Allen Hamilton, which does a lot of business with the US government.

Hirundo, a vendor which says it is building "the first Machine Unlearning Platform to ensure that AI models only know what they should," makes the same argument. The company also notes that its efforts to apply "unlearning" to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B saw a dramatic drop in output that reflects Communist Party of China's preferred censorship, propaganda messaging, or bias. 89.8 percent of the model's output reflected those values before unlearning reduced the incidence to 2.8 percent.

Nous Research did not achieve such dramatic results, but did see an overall reduction in viewpoints deemed to be propaganda.

"On our evaluation, Arete-27B raised its fact score from 2.32 to 2.98 out of 5 and cut answers containing propaganda from 22 percent to 1 percent, in line with the Western models we tested," the company said.

To handle Arete's unlearning, Nous Research says it briefly considered Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra, "but had found evidence that it too had a checkered record on China-related topics."

"We don't know definitively, but theorize that the bias imparted to Nemotron came from working with Chinese open models during the training process," the company said. "We have experienced similar contamination, because the vast majority of high quality open models are Chinese, and only open models have terms of use that permit this kind of tinkering and experimentation."

In the end, the biz tapped Inkling, an open weight model from US-based Thinking Machines Lab, to act as the teaching model.

Nous Research says its model re-education efforts show that the propaganda layer is shallow and, with 50 million tokens worth of supervised learning, is relatively easy to remove. ®

#9931. Singapore says US authorities, and Supermicro, hardly helped investigation of Jensen Huang’s Chinese friend

Seized passport during probe of suspected paperwork fibs that hid server shipments to parts unknown

The government of Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs has revealed it investigated Alice Huang, the woman who is an alleged Chinese intelligence asset and had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and a possible entanglement with troubled server-maker Supermicro. US authorities provided only “limited assistance” in the matter, despite Singapore asking for help.

The Ministry outlined its activities in a statement published late on Thursday, Singapore time.

The document reveals that Singapore’s Police Force (SPF) and Customs agency commenced an investigation into Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, in February 2025.

“The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences,” the Ministry wrote, adding that the exec “was not investigated for espionage.”

Singaporean authorities wanted to know if servers bought by local companies, but exported to Malaysia without ever touching Singaporean soil, might have ended up in a third country.

It is not unusual for Singapore-based companies to acquire goods that never reach the island, because it promotes itself as the ideal spot from which to run an operation that trades across Asia. Singapore does so because it is tiny – the whole nation is the same size as the five boroughs of New York City.

That small size means Singapore restricts the number of datacenters that can operate on its soil.

Those limits are a big reason why Malaysia’s Johor region, which is under 20kms from the border with Singapore and a joint special economic zone, has become a major datacenter province.

Singapore needs deals like that to thrive but works hard to ensure its hospitality is not abused.

Which is why it felt Megaspeed’s activities worthy of investigation.

US authorities were interested too. On 24 June 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security, which regulates sensitive goods subject to export controls, visited Megaspeed in Singapore to check the hardware it bought arrived at its intended destination.

Ms. Huang attended that event and later met the SPF for an interview.

That meeting ended with the SPF impounding her passport, so it could keep her in Singapore while the investigation continued.

As the matter progressed, the SPF suspected perennially troubled server-maker Supermicro had a role in this situation.

Readers may recall that the US Department of Justice indicted two Supermicro execs for conspiring to ship servers to China in contravention of US law. Supermicro investigated the matter and parted ways with three staff who acted improperly. The company has denied ever selling to Megaspeed.

Singaporean authorities say they received only “limited cooperation” from Supermicro, so in July 2025 the office of the nation’s Attorney General asked US authorities for help.

“Since September 2025, SPF has repeated this request on several occasions to the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation,” the statement reveals. “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company.”

In February 2026, the SPF “concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”

But the police did decide that Ms. Huang provided inaccurate information “to downplay her role in Megaspeed.”

“She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country.”

The police returned her passport and Ms. Huang left Singapore on the same day.

The Singaporean statement shows the island nation wants the world to know it does not facilitate sanction-busting activity and takes even the hint of it seriously.

That matters to Nvidia, too, because Singaporean buyers sometimes account for over 20 percent of its quarterly revenue and may continue to do so. Whoever replaces Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO will surely face many questions about the company’s practices. Singapore may just have made answering those queries a little easier. ®

#9929. Newer Models, Same Advantage

Three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

The training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

The combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

OCR models have been moving quickly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

The proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

This distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

DharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

That concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — new architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two new OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

DharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

Processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'

These are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

DharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

The examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

Extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

When a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output

This is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

The operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

Supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

The benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

It is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

What changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

This is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — new architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Three months ago, we showed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

#9928. Developer cleverly shrank 2,600 lines of C into a six-line script but still ending up losing sleep

It wasn't the not-very-legal source code raid that caused it, but a colleague who punted a pager

Working in tech support can be thankless when gormless colleagues leave you sleepless. Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told us that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script.

He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP).

"Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote.

This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases.

"In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the strict proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. "It took me quite some time using WAIS to track it down – the security could have been better – and read the code."

Having found what he needed, Tim wrote his script, which ran overnight to collect data from the telco's switches, tidied up the raw info, and uploaded it to a mainframe.

"It would automatically page me if it couldn't connect to a switch or mainframe after three attempts," he explained.

The script worked fine, but the telco's networks didn't. Tim's pager was soon going off two or three times a night, every night.

After two weeks of interrupted sleep, Tim's manager kindly told him to give the pager to a colleague.

But that colleague habitually left the pager at work, forgot to turn it on, or conveniently placed it out of earshot.

So Tim reluctantly took back the pager and endured another few weeks of nightly interruptions.

How many consecutive sleepless nights have you endured while On Call? If you have enough energy, click here to send your story with On Call so we can share it on a future Friday. ®

InfoQ Homepage News Azure Logic Apps Standard Gets a Local CLI in Preview

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read

Microsoft has released a public preview of a local command-line interface for Azure Logic Apps Standard, shipped as the logicapp extension for the Azure CLI. It adds project creation, workflow authoring, a local runtime, connector and connection management, run inspection, and test scaffolding to a tool that until now only managed deployed apps, so that a Standard workflow can be created, run, and tested without Visual Studio Code.

The extension installs automatically the first time an az logicapp developer command runs on Azure CLI 2.67.0 or later, and adds 19 command groups with 64 commands beside the thirteen existing cloud-management commands, which it leaves untouched. On the authoring side, project create creates or adopts a local project; workflow create, set, export, and validate work on individual workflow.json files with offline validation by default, and runtime start, stop, and show manage a local host on port 7071, launching the Azurite storage emulator when the project is configured for development storage.

The remaining groups reach into running and deployed apps. connector and connection inspect built-in and managed connectors and wire connections into a project or a deployed app, run and trigger history start, wait on, cancel and resubmit executions and download an action’s recorded inputs and outputs, and deployment package produces what the documentation calls a deterministic deployment package. Named context shortcuts hold a target so later commands do not repeat it.

The doctor and test commands say the most about who the tool expects to be typing. runtime doctor only reads: project files, tool versions, cached bundle evidence, loopback ports. It "never installs, downloads, starts, stops, repairs, decrypts settings, changes context, or contacts cloud storage," and it exits 1 for a required failure and 2 when a required check comes back unknown. Testing is split into three steps for the same reason. test create scaffolds a native SDK test project and stops before restoring a package or running anything, test plan writes a preflight report without executing a test, and test run is the only command that builds and runs them, under a deadline. The announcement lists limitations on that last step. In the pull request that added the extension, author Riley Evans goes further: native SDK test code is trusted rather than sandboxed, and the agent bootstrap command does not exist yet.

Sagar Sharma, a Microsoft MVP, wrote on LinkedIn that this is deliberate. The CLI is "literally pitched as adding determinism to local AI-assisted coding": an agent validates, runs, inspects and tests, then repeats until the run is green, and secrets reach it through stdin rather than on the command line. Sharma had already called the CLI the sleeper hit of Microsoft's recent Logic Apps announcements in an earlier write-up, on the grounds that an agent without a deterministic way to validate and run a workflow is guessing. Named contexts, capability discovery and the handling of secrets were his evidence that someone had designed for that case.

Sonny Gillissen, also a Microsoft MVP, put the same point in terms of a team's week. A new hire clones a repository and has a local runtime up "in minutes, instead of hours." A coding assistant drafting a workflow from a business requirement works "with an authoritative shell instead of assumptions." Integration flows get tested from the CI/CD pipeline instead of by hand. He called the CLI a bridge from today's development process to a fully automated one and, in passing, said an agent could test a workflow locally "without ever touching Azure at all."

That passing remark is the one Christos Panagiotidis, a Microsoft MVP and certified trainer, would test first. His pilot plan is explicitly a proposal rather than a report of a run, and its two main cautions come straight from Microsoft's own walkthrough. That walkthrough uses live Azure and Microsoft 365 resources, and some of its commands change deployed connections, so a local run has remote effects, whatever the terminal suggests.

Microsoft itself notes that validation "does not establish authorization or business correctness." Panagiotidis adds a housekeeping point: CLI extensions do not update with the CLI, so anyone comparing results across runs needs the CLI, extension, runtime and project versions recorded next to each result.

Microsoft has said a broader command surface will follow soon. Until then, the designer stays in VS Code. The CLI edits workflow.json directly; it cannot change the state of a running local app, and the pull request's own limits section concedes that Linux CI results prove neither native SDK execution nor execution against live Azure.

#9926. Writing a DSL for high performance parallel programming in OxCaml

Using ASCII waveforms to test hardware designs

The following is part of a series of posts about 2026 summer intern projects—for more, see “What the interns have wrought, special jumbo 2026 edition”

We have a lot of performance-critical SIMD code (single-instruction, multiple-data) running on CPUs across the firm. These are highly parallel programs where you run the same computation across arrays of data, in our case for options pricing or for low-latency risk checks. Because OCaml hasn’t historically exposed SIMD instructions, these programs often involve an inner loop written in fairly esoteric C. Writing these loops requires implementers to think carefully about hardware, and doing performance tuning, such as modifying unroll factors or vector widths, can require major changes to the code. Moreover, these programs are constrained to a specific instruction set. If we were to target a different architecture or a newer processor, we’d have to rewrite the program.

For his summer internship, Sai Konkimalla built a compiler for a domain specific language (DSL) that makes SIMD more ergonomic and widely accessible. The compiler takes advantage of OxCaml features that were only very recently added to the language, such as runtime metaprogramming, to enable users to write a kernel just once as a regular-ish OxCaml function, then compile and run it on multiple architectures.

To help solve the problem of SIMD code being rather difficult to write and maintain, our DSL uses the SPMD, or “single program, multiple data” programming model. As opposed to SIMD intrinsics, SPMD is higher level and not tied to a specific instruction set. We might normally think of higher-level languages as slower, but with SPMD, a higher level of abstraction lets the compiler make better decisions about how to optimally use the underlying hardware. This ability can lead to significantly faster code.

SPMD was popularized by CUDA (for Nvidia GPUs) and ISPC (for Intel CPUs). In this model, you write a program describing what happens at each index of a loop, then the compiler converts it into a parallel computation. For example, in CUDA:

Notice how there’s no loop here: you only define the loop body, and the compiler decides how to run it. In CUDA, when you launch a kernel on a GPU, you can declare how many blocks of threads to run and the GPU will schedule them accordingly.

In ISPC, foreach also abstracts away how the loop is actually executed:

In both cases, the compiler translates the code into low-level SIMD instructions. Not specifying the exact instructions also means SPMD programs can benefit from future hardware improvements. If we get a new, faster CPU with a different instruction set, the SPMD compiler can seamlessly compile existing code to it.

Let’s go over an example of the DSL that Sai implemented. We start by defining the kernel’s signature, including its output type, input types, and the dimension of the output:

In this example, we’re writing a kernel that takes in two F32 slices and returns one F32 slice.

Future work on a ppx syntax extension will make it possible to rewrite the above simply as:

Note the let open (val Spmd.open_ graph) in. This brings the DSL operations which construct a computational graph into scope. You can think of the graph value as proof that you’re in the graph-construction phase, not the runtime of the generated program. (Bonsai uses a similar trick for creating its incremental graph.)

Like CUDA, we don’t write the kernel as a loop. Instead, the developer writes a function that computes a single entry of the output slice, and the SPMD compiler generates code to loop over the output slice and compute the value at each index.

You may wonder why we loop over the output and not the inputs. Looping over the output is easier to model because each iteration writes to exactly one location, so iterations can be easily vectorized, reordered, or parallelized. If we were to loop over the inputs, different iterations could write to the same output entry. The compiler would then have to reason about whether the writes could be re-ordered. By guaranteeing that each output entry is written exactly once, we can avoid this complexity.

One wrinkle with Sai’s project is that we wanted to execute the SPMD compiler at runtime. Runtime compilation (often called just-in-time or JIT compilation) is when the compiler generates code while the program is running. This gives us two main advantages: we don’t have to worry about building for all potential target architectures at compile time, and we can use data obtained at runtime for optimizations.

That latter point is especially important for generating high-performance code. When executing at runtime, the compiler has more data that it can use to optimize the code than it would when executing ahead-of-time. For example, our compiler can use runtime data to compile away branch instructions, which can slow down execution by consuming CPU resources.

To implement our JIT compiler, we used runtime metaprogramming, a feature that lets us generate, compile, and evaluate OxCaml code at runtime by using the OxCaml compiler as a library. As far as we know, Sai’s project was the first real program at Jane Street to use it. (He discovered some bugs in its implementation and helped report/reproduce them for the OxCaml team.)

Let’s take a look at an example that illustrates the power of compiling at runtime. In this code, we match on the metric to choose which algorithm to execute:

With a normal OCaml program, this would create a branch and two code paths. Every time we execute this code, we’d have to spend time evaluating the branch and picking the right code path.

With the SPMD compiler, we can compile after we know the value of metric. Then the JIT compiler can evaluate the branch during compilation and produce more efficient code. For example, here’s the intermediate representation that the code gets compiled into:

Notice how we don’t branch on metric in the emitted code. Because the compiler knows the value of metric, it can emit just the chosen algorithm.

Sai started his project by working on the compiler’s front end. The front end takes the kernel definition that we saw above and translates it into the following GADT that models a directed acyclic graph (DAG):

(The 'u type variable in this GADT declares the expression’s rate, which indicates whether an expression is the same for every index in the entire output slice (uniform) or may change at each element in the slice (varying). In other words, it signals which pieces of your computation only need to be computed once and which pieces need to be computed per index.)

Sai’s first task was to add support for numeric data types such as I8, I16, I64, U8–U64 and F64, including arithmetic operations and conversion operators. After that, he started implementing booleans and control flow constructs. Unlike most conventional programming languages, SPMD has some nuances to its control flow. Instead of a single if construct, SPMD has three separate constructs all designed for parallel execution:

if_var lets you branch on data that varies per index (i.e., per SIMD lane). In the code below, the if_var allows the user to guard code that should only be run when g happens to be positive:

The plain if_ can’t do that, because the condition is a bool# uniform and therefore it must be the same value for all lanes.

select and if_var are similar in that they both take in a condition of type bool# varying. Where the two constructs differ is in how the branches are evaluated. With if_var, the compiler can decide whether to execute the branch that is not chosen by the condition, whereas with select, both branches are always evaluated. Further, if if_var executes an untaken branch, any potential side effects, such as raising exceptions, will not be observable. So select true 1 (1/0) will raise an exception, but {if,if_var} true 1 (1/0) will not.

Usually, a high-performance JIT compiler would target a low-level language such as assembly or LLVM IR, which necessitates thinking quite hard about complicated details such as registers, pointers, and so on. Luckily, we didn’t have to do this, since we could use metaprogramming to emit OxCaml code. This also lets us rely on optimizations in the OxCaml compiler, saving us from having to implement them ourselves.

OxCaml’s metaprogramming features let us explicitly generate OxCaml code at runtime using quotes and splices. A quotation represents an OxCaml expression that is created at runtime and will be evaluated at a later time. For example, <[if Random.bool () then 42 else 5]> represents an unevaluated expression of type int, so the quotation itself has type <[int]> expr. Once this expression is evaluated, its result will be an int.

Quotations can be interpolated into other quotations by splicing ($):

So rather than writing the standard recursive power function that computes x^n:

you can write a power_expr function that creates a quoted expression that will compute x^n for a given n, effectively inlining and optimizing the recursive function into a single expression. This is a form of partial evaluation where we’re able to take a function and produce a much faster version specialized to a particular value of n.

Sai’s backend walked the DAG and emitted OxCaml code for each node. For instance, the backend emits the following quoted OxCaml code for arithmetic expressions:

If we were to compile a basic kernel such as:

we’d get a DAG that represents the arithmetic operations, and use that to generate quoted OxCaml code:

Sai implemented these emitters for all of the node types in the DAG, such as the if_, if_var and select control flow constructs.

At this point, Sai needed to validate that his JIT implementation was both fast and correct. One strategy he used was to compare the JIT against a reference implementation. We had previously implemented an interpreter that took the front-end representation and directly executed it. While extremely slow, we could be fairly confident that the interpreter would have the correct behavior, so could be used to verify that the JIT was also correct.

Sai wrote four example programs, including an implementation of Newton’s square root algorithm and a kernel adapted from some production code, in plain OxCaml, C with AVX2 intrinsics, C with AVX512 intrinsics, and as an SPMD kernel (which could be either executed by the interpreter or JIT compiled). Each combination was benchmarked on inputs of various sizes.

Sai also worked on an extensive test suite for all of the different language features and edge-cases. This suite included a test that generated random inputs with Quickcheck generators, then ran those inputs on the four example programs. Their outputs were cross-checked and compared bit by bit. He also wrote tests confirming that the code didn’t allocate on the heap.

The benchmarks found that the JIT was much faster than the interpreter. However, the JIT was about the same speed (or slightly slower) than the manual OxCaml code and significantly slower than the C implementations. This wasn’t that surprising, since we hadn’t implemented any real optimizations or tuning in the compiler. Naturally, this needed to change if we wanted to catch up to the C implementations.

Sai then started looking at adding optimizations to the compiler. With the current compilation pipeline, this would have been slightly painful. Our front end representation was not designed to be easily analyzed or optimized. While that wouldn’t have necessarily stopped us from doing analysis, it’s often a better idea to add an intermediate representation (IR) that is more amenable to optimization. Sai implemented an IR based on A-normal form (ANF), a format where each intermediate value gets its own variable. This is the IR that we saw in the previous section about optimizing away control flow:

The IR is more verbose but easier to analyze. For example, because all intermediate values are assigned a variable, it becomes easy to remove dead code; just look if an intermediate value is used anywhere after its definition.

Sai designed this IR with a key design principle in mind: Generating the final OxCaml code from the IR should be a trivial process. Any interesting compilation logic should end up explicitly represented in the IR.

One instance of this principle shows up in how we model loops. As we mentioned before, kernels only declare what we do on each loop iteration, not how we loop over the code itself.

But in the IR, we explicitly specify the loop, as well as load/store logic. That way, the optimizer can reason about how to re-order or unroll loops. For example, the above kernel would produce the following IR:

The optimizer can analyze this IR and see that v1 and v2 do not depend on i and therefore can be lifted out of the loop:

It can also rewrite the loop to process 4 elements at a time, which reduces the amount of branching in the code.

By making the IR fairly explicit, we’re able to reason about—and therefore optimize—the code effectively.

Like with the previous backend implementation, Sai put in a lot of work to validate the correctness of the new compilation path. He added the new backend to the existing cross-validation logic across the test suite, then added expect tests that printed the IR and the emitted OxCaml for various examples, which helped us confirm that the behavior was exactly as expected.

Once we were confident that the new IR-based path was correct, Sai deleted the previous backend.

With the current implementation, the IR backend generates essentially the same code as the first JIT, so the two perform about the same.

However, optimizations are now significantly easier to add. We’re currently working on adding vectorization and constant hoisting to the compiler. Preliminary benchmarks have found that these changes result in code that is on-par with our C AVX2 implementation.

We’re also working on adding scheduling. Scheduling lets users customize how the kernel loops over the code with a sophisticated set of transformations like “split this loop into 8 piece chunks, vectorize these chunks, then unroll by 4”. Intelligent scheduling is important for getting the maximum possible performance out of the kernel. Eventually these schedules could also be auto-generated and benchmarked, so that the compiler can find the optimal one for your kernel.

Nicholas is a software engineer and technical writer at Jane Street. He has written multiple blog posts about chili oil.

#9925. Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

Robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

But you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

And that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

Grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

We have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

And while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right)

Components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

Press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :

The data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

This release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most important next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

👉 Build a Grabette (GitHub) · Process your data (HF Space) · Contribute to the dataset

#9924. Someone's impersonating this blog

I was googling the name of my website, as one does occasionally, and was surprised to see a link to one of my blog posts on mataroa.site. At first I figured it was just an alternate domain name for mataroa.blog, but no, when you type mataroa.site into your browser, it shows you my blog. It's the only thing that's hosted there.

My next thought was that someone bought me a URL, but that can't be the case either: using a custom domain on mataroa requires a premium account, which I don't have. For anything but a plain redirect, I would have needed to set up the A record my end.

I then realized that the version of my blog on that site doesn't have the latest post. The most recent update on the homepage is my Aug 21 entry. When you scroll down and start clicking some of the older links, you get 404 pages. You also get a 404 if you try to post a comment, load the RSS feed or view standalone pages like the AI statement.

Someone scraped my blog and created a website to impersonate me. They're also impersonating mataroa, since using the name implies some sort of official connection.

They're re-hosting the stolen images on their own server, and they all have a watermark. Bizarrely, the watermark is mattbee.mataroa.blog, my real URL. I assume this is to somehow make it seem legitimate, like it's an officially-sanctioned mirror, but I don't know who they think is going to care. It's not like they're stealing from a site with name recognition.

When you view the source of a blog post, it's identical to the rendered HTML except that there are two Cloudflare scripts at the bottom, one to obfuscate the mailto: link in the footer (which doesn't work1) and one for analytics.

When you view the source of the index, there's a hidden link at the bottom to a Chinese github.io page for a website cloning tool.

I have no idea why I was targeted for impersonation. It should be obvious this isn't a high-value website.2 It's a personal blog where I write what's relevant to me, and that rarely overlaps with anything other people care about. If the subject matter didn't tip them off, it should be clear from the 0 comments on most posts that this is not an enterprise ripe for monetization.

If they just wanted a fake blog to scam adsense, surely a large language model would happily spew out more SEO-friendly slop than anything I have to offer. If their goal was to leech off the popularity of mataroa, why not impersonate one of the blogs with multiple front-page appearances on the orange website? Surely they have more SEO juice than me. Nothing about this makes any sense.

Anyway, the URL is registered with Namecheap, so I sent them an abuse report. I have no idea if they'll act on it. They don't seem to have a good track record of giving a shit unless the content is actually hosted with them.

It's hosted with Cloudflare, and the abuse reporting form they insist you use straight-up doesn't work. Click "Submit an abuse report" and it'll take you to a completely blank page. Very encouraging.

I'd have to dox myself to do a DMCA takedown, and I don't have the legal resources to do anything when it gets ignored. So if neither evil corporation cares to do anything, I guess I can just get fucked. I figure the best thing I can do to protect myself is document everything here. If you see a link to mataroa.site, it's not affiliated with me or mataroa. It seems like it isn't set up to scam people or distribute malware at the moment, but it probably will in the future. Be careful.

The index page also has a meta tag with a verification code for mitgo.com, a fake-looking website with some word salad identifying it as some kind of ad/SEO scamming platform or service. Will try to investigate this further.

Sorry for... checking to see if your website started working? Too many times? I guess??? 🤷‍♀️

It does, I had just forgotten to enable javascript. ↩

#9923. Microsoft services restored to all customers, company says it's 'deeply sorry'

The company restored service to email and other Microsoft 365 and related services to all customers by Friday night

In Australia, they called it it the “Microsoft long weekend” – an outage so pervasive it just about made Friday a write-off at organizations which rely on Redmond’s online services, especially Exchange Online. Service was finally restored to all customers early Saturday morning GMT, according to the company's official Microsoft 365 Status account on X.

Around 0600 UTC on Saturday, the company posted: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center." The company also said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners."

As The Register reported, the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services.

The software giant said the outage impacted Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional.

The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.”

As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.”

Microsoft’s status page includes only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order:

We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online;

We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected;

We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability;

We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances;

We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery;

Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected.

Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon.

“We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.”

Hopefully, Australia and other countries in nearby time zones won’t be the only ones to get an unscheduled long weekend. ®Updated at 0056 Sunday UTC to reflect the end of the outage.

Updated to add at 2144 UTCRedmond still claims that the situation is in the process of stabilizing with no estimate for when everything might get back to normal. "As infrastructure stabilizes, we're still draining queued messages and rebalancing traffic, so customers may see improved sign-in/access while delivery and processing continue to catch up," it writes on its status page. "We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet. Service access can recover before mail flow fully normalizes." The company issued its latest status update at 2002 UTC and promises another update by Saturday at 0000 UTC.

Updated to add at 1300 UTCMicrosoft says it's seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with "broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. We're also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific, although some users may continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure."

Updated to add at 1200 UTCThe latest status update at 12:00 PM UTC admits users are still "unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services."

#9922. Bringing Nunchaku 4-bit Diffusion Inference to Diffusers

Large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs. Quantization is a powerful solution to this problem, and Diffusers already integrates several quantization backends such as bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, and Quanto, which we covered in Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers.

Most of these backends are weight-only. This means that they store the weights in low precision and dequantize them back to high precision at compute time. This reduces memory usage significantly, but it usually does not make inference faster, and can even add a small latency overhead.

SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach. It runs the main transformer layers with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), reducing memory while also speeding up the denoising loop. The details are covered below, but until now, using these checkpoints required a separate inference library.

With current Diffusers, loading a Nunchaku checkpoint is as simple as calling from_pretrained(), with no local CUDA compilation required thanks to the kernels package. In addition, the companion diffuse-compressor toolkit lets you quantize new architectures yourself and publish them as regular Diffusers repositories.

First, install the requirements. You need a recent version of Diffusers and the Hugging Face kernels package:

Then load a pre-quantized pipeline like any other Diffusers model:

No custom pipeline class or separate inference engine is needed, and there is nothing to compile locally. The NVFP4 kernels are downloaded from the Hub through the Nunchaku Lite kernels page the first time they are used. This checkpoint pairs a Nunchaku NVFP4 transformer with a bitsandbytes NF4 text encoder, and generates a 1024x1024 image in about 1.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 with a peak memory usage of about 12 GB, compared with about 24 GB for the BF16 pipeline. You can find more details about the Nunchaku Lite checkpoint format in the official Diffusers documentation.

NVFP4 checkpoints require an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, B200). For earlier generations, use the INT4 variants. See the hardware support table below for details.

SVDQuant is the quantization method behind Nunchaku, its reference CUDA inference engine. Standard 4-bit quantization is difficult for diffusion transformers because both weights and activations contain large outliers. SVDQuant handles this by moving activation outliers into the weights, representing the hardest part of each weight matrix with a small 16-bit low-rank branch, and quantizing the remaining residual to 4 bits. Nunchaku makes this fast with fused kernels for the 4-bit path and the low-rank branch.

The original Nunchaku engine gets much of its speed from model-specific fused execution paths, such as fused QKV projections and fused GELU/MLP kernels. Those optimizations are tied to each architecture's module layout and checkpoint format, so supporting a new model family usually requires model-specific integration work.

Nunchaku Lite is the new integration path in Diffusers. With it, Diffusers can load Nunchaku-style checkpoints without a custom pipeline or a separate inference engine. Under the hood, Nunchaku Lite patches the relevant nn.Linear modules of a stock Diffusers model with runtime SVDQ/AWQ linear layers before the checkpoint is loaded. The CUDA kernels come from the Hub through the kernels package. Two kernel families are used:

The trade-off is that, without architecture-specific fused kernels and modules, Nunchaku Lite cannot match the speedup of the original Nunchaku engine. However, the bare-bones implementation still delivers around 30% speedup while retaining the same level of VRAM reduction.

If you have used bitsandbytes or torchao in Diffusers, the mechanics will feel familiar. A Nunchaku Lite model repository is an ordinary Diffusers repository. The only special part is a quantization_config block inside the transformer's config.json:

This config tells Diffusers which modules were quantized, which scheme they use, and which Nunchaku Lite runtime layer to instantiate (SVDQW4A4Linear or AWQW4A16Linear).

Because the quantized model keeps the exact module structure of the dense one, everything downstream (schedulers, LoRA loading hooks, offloading, torch.compile) sees a normal Diffusers model.

Nunchaku Lite uses different kernel variants depending on the GPU generation and checkpoint precision:

Volta and Hopper GPUs are currently not supported by the 4-bit kernels. The quantizer validates the GPU's CUDA capability at load time and raises a clear error instead of producing incorrect outputs.

Nunchaku Lite can be combined with other Diffusers memory and speed optimizations.

torch.compile. Compiling the transformer improves the end-to-end speedup from 1.35x to 1.8x:

Quantized text encoders. The transformer is not the only component with a large memory footprint. Text encoders such as T5 or Qwen3 can occupy several gigabytes on their own. Further quantizing the text encoder with bitsandbytes NF4 reduces peak VRAM by about 22% in our benchmark.

Offloading. Diffusers offloading helpers such as enable_model_cpu_offload() and enable_sequential_cpu_offload() work as usual if you need to fit the pipeline onto a smaller GPU.

All numbers below were measured on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell) at 1024x1024 using rootonchair/ERNIE-Image-Turbo-nunchaku-lite-int4-bnb4-text-encoder.

As shown above, Nunchaku reduces peak VRAM by up to 50% while still improving latency by roughly 30%. The remaining overhead comes largely from extra kernel launches, which torch.compile can mitigate, bringing the full pipeline down to 1.68 s, or 1.8x faster than the BF16 baseline.

Nunchaku Lite support in Diffusers is architecture-agnostic, and the diffuse-compressor toolkit provides an end-to-end SVDQuant workflow for Diffusers models: calibrate, quantize, package, and publish.

Below, we walk through quantizing FLUX.2 Klein 4B as an example. It covers the main steps: inspect the model, calibrate and quantize the transformer, package the result as a Diffusers pipeline, then verify and push it to the Hub. The full tutorial covers every flag in detail.

The generic scanner walks the model and decides what to target: compatible linears inside the repeated transformer-block stack become SVDQ W4A4 targets, recognized modulation linears become AWQ W4A16 targets, and everything else stays dense.

Always read this report before quantizing. For FLUX.2 Klein 4B, the expected result is 100 SVDQ targets, 3 AWQ targets, and 6 dense outer linears, with no missing patterns or duplicate names.

The following command runs SVDQuant on the transformer and writes the quantized checkpoint to outputs/checkpoints/svdq-int4_r32-flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors:

Replace --precision int4 with nvfp4 to build Blackwell-native weights.

The converter combines the quantized transformer with the base pipeline's other components, writes the compact nunchaku_lite configuration into transformer/config.json, and can optionally convert text encoders to NF4:

Once the outputs look good, run pipe.push_to_hub("your-name/your-model-nunchaku-lite-int4"). Other users can then load it with the same from_pretrained() pattern shown above.

Note that the generic path assumes the architecture can be quantized without structural rewrites. For additional speedup, the original Nunchaku engine rewrites groups of Diffusers layers as fused modules. The generic path cannot infer these changes on its own, such as combining separate Q, K, and V projections into one module or splitting a fused projection across several modules.

FLUX.1-dev's QKV projection is a concrete example. Diffusers defines three separate modules:

The Nunchaku FLUX module combines those layers into one quantized to_qkv module:

This grouped module is required because Nunchaku's fused operator consumes the QKV projection, Q/K normalization, and rotary embeddings together. By comparison, the default Diffusers path executes them separately:

The Nunchaku path supplies the grouped projection, normalization modules, and rotary embeddings to one fused operator:

This is the structural rewrite that the generic path cannot infer. Diffusers has three destination modules with to_q, to_k, and to_v parameter prefixes, while Nunchaku has one grouped module under to_qkv. A model-specific target config or adapter must state that the Q, K, and V parameters should be concatenated along the output dimension, in that order, and loaded into to_qkv.

Structural rewrites like these are described by a model-specific target config during quantization and handled by a small runtime adapter when the checkpoint is loaded. The FLUX.2 Klein 4B quantization script provides a concrete target-config example for producing a structurally rewritten checkpoint, while rootonchair/nunchaku-lite provides the runtime adapters needed to load grouped QKV tensors, split fused projections, and other fused operations. For the complete workflow, you can check the Adding A New Model guide.

To get started right away, check out the following repositories:

Nunchaku's SVDQuant kernels are one of the most effective ways to run diffusion transformers efficiently on consumer hardware, and they are now natively supported in Diffusers. Pre-quantized checkpoints load with from_pretrained(), and the diffuse-compressor toolkit makes it possible to quantize new architectures without waiting for engine support. By quantizing both weights and activations, the W4A4 path lowers memory use while improving denoising latency, keeping image quality close to the BF16 original.

If you quantize and publish a new model, we would love to hear about it. Share it on the Hub and let us know! If you have any questions about this feature, feel free to join our Discord.

To learn more, check out the following resources:

Thanks to the Diffusers maintainers for reviews and guidance throughout the integration, and to the MIT HAN Lab / Nunchaku team for the original SVDQuant work. Thanks to Marc Sun for providing feedback on the blog post. Thanks to Álvaro Somoza for trying out nunchaku-lite and for providing feedback.

rootonchair is also grateful to SilverAI for supporting this work and providing the environment in which much of this development took place.

#9920. C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute

ISO working group faces a fight over runtime checks, complexity, and the language's release timetable

The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature.

Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup, who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself.

The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language.

In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies.

The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay.

Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior.

Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel.

Developers have proposed adding Contracts  to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults.

But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal (P2900) that made it into C++26.

“The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested, and could be more effectively implemented as a library.

Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig, a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself.

“The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post.

The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust. Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language.

Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers.

“Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust."

Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself.

“The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.”

With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history  – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”)

ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final.

According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy, the group faces a number of choices.

They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts.

Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology.

Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®
