#9914. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

Extract text and tables from document images

#9913. Probabilistic data structures in Go

Probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? Which items appear most often? Unlike deterministic structures like sets and frequency tables, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can drastically reduce memory usage.

In this post, we'll talk about what probabilistic structures are, how they work, and what kinds of guarantees they provide. I'll also introduce unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go. It's simple (the core logic for each data structure is 100–300 LOC), fast (usually several times faster than other implementations), and has no dependencies except for the standard library.

Bloom filter • Count-min sketch • HyperLogLog • T-digest • Top-k

A Bloom filter is a set that trades certainty for space. It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't actually store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

For example, a regular set with 1,000,000 distinct 8-byte strings takes about 64 MB. A Bloom filter for the same strings, with a 1% false positive rate, uses only 1.24 MB (about 10 bits per item) — that's 50 times smaller. The size of the filter doesn't depend on the item size, so the difference gets even bigger with longer strings.

A Bloom filter often resides in memory and helps minimize expensive I/O operations such as disk reads or network calls. You check if an item is in the filter, and if the answer is "no", you skip the costly lookup. If the answer is "yes", you still have to perform the lookup because it might be a false positive.

The filter is sized for the given number of items with a given false positive rate. You can add more, but the false positive rate will go up.

You can add an item to a Bloom filter and check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them.

Bloom filter1 is a large array of m bits, all set to zero at first. To add an item, you compute k hash values for it and set the k bits at those positions:

To check if an item is in the filter, you compute the same k hashes and check if all k bits are set:

The k bits are randomly distributed throughout the entire array. When the filter is larger than the CPU cache, each bit access could result in a cache miss, so a lookup may wait on memory k times.

Unsure uses a blocked Bloom filter2. The bit array is divided into 512-bit blocks, each matching the size of a CPU cache line. When you add or check an item, it is hashed once: part of the hash selects a block, and the rest selects k bits within that block. Each add or check only accesses one cache line, so the filter stays fast even when it's very large.

In a blocked Bloom filter, some blocks end up with more items than others, which increases the false positive rate. To make up for this, the filter needs to be a bit larger. Compared to a standard Bloom filter, it uses about 3% more memory at a 1% false positive rate, 8% more at 0.1%, and 15% more at 0.01%.

The filter uses the local wyhash3 implementation for hashing. It performs roughly the same as xxh34 but has a much simpler implementation, without SIMD or assembly.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks5, comparing unsure to bits-and-blooms6 (a classic Bloom filter) and gloom7 (a blocked one) (ns/op, lower is better):

Memory, bits per item at 10M items (lower is better):

Unsure is about 4× faster than bits-and-blooms and 2× faster than gloom, using 1–8% more memory than bits-and-blooms and 4–10% less than gloom.

Space/time trade-offs in hash coding with allowable errors by Burton H. Bloom, 1970. ↩︎

Cache-, hash-, and space-efficient Bloom filters by Felix Putze et al., 2009. ↩︎

Reference wyhash implementation by Wang Yi. ↩︎

Reference xxHash implementation by Yann Collet. ↩︎

bits-and-blooms/bloom by Daniel Lemire. ↩︎

A count-min sketch is a frequency table that trades accuracy for space. It tells you approximately how many times each item has appeared. The estimate is never less than the actual count, but it can be higher. The sketch doesn't actually store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular map of per-item counts.

For example, a regular map counting 1,000,000 distinct 8-byte strings takes about 64 MB. A count-min sketch for the same strings, with estimates within 0.01% of the total count (with 99% probability), uses only 0.55 MB — that's 116 times smaller. The size of the sketch doesn't depend on the number of distinct items or their size, only on the accuracy you choose. So the difference gets even bigger with more or longer strings.

A count-min sketch is useful when you want to track how many times an item shows up in a large stream of events. It's often used to check if something has happened a certain number of times, like rate-limiting an IP after X requests or sending an alert after an error happens Y times. A sketch can also help decide if a key is worth keeping in the cache given how often it was requested.

The sketch uses two settings: epsilon ε and delta δ. If the actual count for any given item is X and the total of all counts is N, then the estimated count for this item will usually be between X and X+ε·N. However, rarely (with a probability of δ) the estimate could be even higher.

For example, if ε is 0.001, δ is 0.01, and N is 1 million, then the estimate could be off by up to 1,000 (ε·N) with at least 99% probability (1−δ), and by more than 1,000 with at most 1% probability (δ).

The counting error in a sketch depends on the total of all counts, not on each individual item. Therefore, frequent items are estimated more or less accurately relative to their count, but rare items are not — the absolute error is too high for them.

You can increase the per-item counter in a sketch and get the estimated count for an item, but you cannot decrease a counter or iterate over the items.

Count-min sketch8 is a table of counters with d rows and w columns, all starting at zero. Each row uses its own hash function that maps an item to one of the w counters. To add an item, you increment its counter in each row:

To estimate an item's count, you take the smallest value from its d counters:

With w = e/ε columns, each counter's error is at most ε·N, with probability at least 1 − 1/e. If you use d = ln(1/δ) rows, the chance that all d of the item's counters exceed its true count by more than ε·N is ≤ δ.

Unsure uses a conservative update. When you add n to an item, it first finds the current estimate E (the smallest counter), then increases only the counters that are below E+n, leaving the larger ones unchanged. This keeps the same accuracy guarantee, but the actual error is about 2× lower. The tradeoff is that counts can't be decreased.

Counters are 32-bit instead of the usual 64-bit, so the sketch uses 2× less memory. The item is hashed once, and each row gets its own position from that hash by salting it (multiplying by a random per-row constant).

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks9, comparing unsure to BoomFilters10 (a classic count-min sketch with 64-bit counters) (ns/op, lower is better):

Accuracy at ε=0.0001, N=10M additions over 1M distinct items, mean overestimate (lower is better):

Unsure is about 1.5× faster for Add and 4× faster for Count, using 2× less memory with 2–2.7× lower error.

An improved data stream summary: the count-min sketch and its applications by Graham Cormode and S. Muthukrishnan, 2005. ↩︎

tylertreat/BoomFilters by Tyler Treat. ↩︎

HyperLogLog is a unique items counter that trades accuracy for space. It tells you approximately how many distinct items it has seen, no matter how many times each one appeared. HyperLogLog (also called a sketch from here on) doesn't actually store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

For example, a regular set of 1,000,000 distinct 8-byte strings takes about 64 MB. A HyperLogLog sketch counting the same strings with about 0.8% error uses only 16 KB — that's almost 4,000 times smaller. The size of the sketch doesn't depend on the number of items or their size, only on the accuracy you choose. A 16 KB sketch counts a billion items as accurately as a thousand.

HyperLogLog is useful when you need to count unique things in a large stream: unique visitors to a website, unique search queries per day, or distinct values in a database column.

You can merge sketches to gather data from multiple machines or segments (like by hour, page, or region). When you merge two sketches, you get the total number of unique items from both, without counting shared items twice.

The sketch has one setting: the precision p, which gives a relative standard error (stdErr) of 1.04/√(2^p). A common default is p=14, which gives 0.81% error.

The error is relative to the count, so the standard error is the same 0.81% for a thousand items or a billion.

You can add items to a sketch, get the estimated count, and merge sketches. You cannot check if a specific item was added, remove items, or list them.

HyperLogLog11 is based on a simple observation. If you hash items to random bit strings, about half of them start with 1, a quarter with 01, an eighth with 001, and so on. Seeing a hash with k leading zeros suggests there were about 2^(k+1) distinct items. Duplicates hash to the same value, so they don't affect the result.

A single observation is unreliable, so the sketch divides the items into m = 2^p groups, where p is the selected precision. The first p bits of the hash pick a group (a register), and the register keeps the highest rank (leading zeros plus one) it has seen in the rest of the hash:

The count is estimated from all the registers together, using a harmonic mean of 2^register. The standard error is about 1.04/√m. Merging two sketches is just taking the maximum value from each pair of registers.

The original estimator is biased when dealing with small counts (up to a few times m), so in these cases it uses a different formula called linear counting. This switch creates a sudden change in error, and some implementations (like HyperLogLog++12) address it by using large tables of bias corrections based on real data.

Unsure uses the improved estimator by Otmar Ertl13. Instead of a harmonic mean of the registers, it works from a histogram: how many registers have value 0, value 1, and so on. A formula applied to the histogram gives an accurate estimate for any number of items, from zero to billions, so there's no need for a separate formula for small counts or for correction tables.

The sketch updates the histogram whenever registers change. Most adds don't change any registers, so this is almost free. Counting always takes the same amount of time, no matter how big the sketch is. Other implementations scan all the registers on every count, which takes from microseconds to milliseconds.

Registers are one byte each, and the histogram has 64 four-byte counters (256 bytes). The item is hashed once with wyhash, and the 64-bit hash is split into the register index and the rank.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks14, comparing unsure to axiom15 (HyperLogLog with LogLog-Beta estimator and sparse mode) (ns/op, lower is better):

Accuracy at p=14 (0.81% standard error), relative RMSE over 100 sketches (lower is better):

Memory at p=14 after adding the given number of distinct items (lower is better):

Unsure adds about as fast as axiom, counts 270–83,000× faster, and merges 2.3–2.9× faster, with the same accuracy and memory for counts above the number of registers. When there are fewer items than registers, axiom's sparse mode makes it more accurate and compact.

HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm by Philippe Flajolet et al., 2007. ↩︎

HyperLogLog in practice by Stefan Heuleet et al., 2013. ↩︎

New cardinality estimation algorithms for HyperLogLog sketches by Otmar Ertl, 2017. ↩︎

A t-digest is a summary of a stream of numbers that trades accuracy for space. It can give you an approximate median, 99th percentile, or any other quantile of the data. It can also estimate what fraction of the numbers are below a certain value (the CDF). The digest doesn't actually store the numbers, so it's much more compact than a sorted list.

For example, to find the exact 99th percentile of 1,000,000 numbers, you'd have to keep all of them. With 64-bit floats, that takes 8 MB. A t-digest estimates the same percentile within about 0.03% of the rank (between the 98.97th and the 99.03rd percentile) using only 8 KB — 1,000 times smaller. The size of the digest doesn't depend on the number of values, only on the accuracy you choose. An 8 KB digest summarizes a billion values as well as a million.

A t-digest is useful when you need quantiles over a large stream: latency percentiles for a service, the distribution of request sizes or prices, or the outlier thresholds in sensor data.

You can merge digests to gather data from multiple machines or segments (like by hour, endpoint, or region). A merged digest estimates the percentiles of all values, but with less accuracy than individual digests do.

The digest has one setting: the compression δ, which limits the number of centroids (see How it works below) to δ+2. A common default is δ=100, which takes 8 KB. Increasing δ uses more memory but reduces estimation error.

The error is measured in ranks: a rank error of 0.03% at quantile q=0.99 means the value returned by Quantile(0.99) is somewhere between the 98.97th and the 99.03rd percentile of the actual values. Tail estimates, such as q=0.99 or q=0.999, are more accurate than the median (q=0.5).

You can add numbers to a digest, estimate quantiles and the CDF, and merge digests. You cannot remove numbers or list them.

T-digest16 summarizes the numbers as a sorted list of centroids. Each centroid has a mean and a weight — the number of values it represents. To estimate a quantile, the digest finds the centroids around the requested rank and interpolates between their means.

The trick is in how big the centroids are allowed to grow. A scale function k(q) maps a quantile q to a number from -δ/4 to δ/4, and each centroid may only span 1 unit of k: if a centroid covers the quantiles from q₁ to q₂, then k(q₂) − k(q₁) ≤ 1.

The arcsine scale function, k(q) = δ/(2π)·asin(2q-1), is steep near q=0 and q=1 and flat near the median. This means the centroids it produces are larger in the center and smaller at the ends:

With 1M values and δ=100, the centroids around the median hold about 27,000 values each, those around the 99th percentile about 5,000, and the outermost ones about 500. This keeps the error near the tails small.

Unsure is the merging t-digest from the Dunning and Ertl paper. New values go to a buffer of 5·δ numbers. When the buffer is full, the digest sorts it and merges it with the centroids (already sorted) in a single pass, building new centroids from left to right as long as each one fits within its span of k. Every other pass goes right to left, so that neither tail ends up with fuller centroids. Quantile, CDF and Merge flush the buffer first.

The centroids are kept in two fixed arrays of δ+2 entries (the current list and the next one being built), along with the cumulative weights for a binary search in Quantile and CDF. With δ=100, that's 16·102·2 + 8·103 bytes for the centroids, and 8·500 bytes for the buffer, about 8 KB in total.

Centroids with weight 1 are treated as exact values rather than spread around their mean, and the exact minimum and maximum are used at the ends. So digests with few values give exact results, and Quantile(0) and Quantile(1) are always exact.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks17, comparing unsure to influxdata18 (merging t-digest with the same scale function) (ns/op, lower is better):

Accuracy at δ=100, mean rank error over 1M normal values (lower is better):

Memory at δ=100 (lower is better): unsure 8.5 KB, influxdata 14.4 KB.

Unsure adds values about 1.8× faster than influxdata, queries at the same speed, merges 7–9× faster, and uses 40% less memory at about the same accuracy.

Computing extremely accurate quantiles using t-digests by Ted Dunning and Otmar Ertl, 2019. ↩︎

A Top-k sketch finds the k most frequent items in a stream (the "heavy hitters"), along with their approximate counts. It uses a fixed amount of memory based only on k, no matter how many different items are in the stream.

To find the exact top items, you'd have to count every unique item, for example with a map of per-item counts. With millions of distinct items, that takes tens or hundreds of megabytes. A Top-k sketch for the top 1000 items takes about 360 KB, and it usually finds all of them.

A Top-k sketch is useful when you want to identify the "hottest" data: the most requested URLs, the most active users, or the most common search queries. Unlike a count-min sketch, it keeps the actual items, so it can list them.

Top returns up to k items, from the most frequent to the least frequent. Counts are estimates: they're usually exact for the most frequent items, but may be slightly lower than the actual count for less common items.

The sketch works best when the stream is skewed, meaning a few items appear much more often than the others. This is common in real situations. If all items are about equally frequent, there is no clear top k, and the results become less accurate.

You can add items to the sketch and get the top items with their counts, but you can't decrease counts or check items that aren't in the top k.

HeavyKeeper19 is a table of buckets that estimates item counts. It has d rows and w columns, and each item maps to one bucket in each row. Each bucket holds a fingerprint of the item and a count. To add an item, you update its bucket in each row:

The item's estimated count is the largest count among its buckets. Frequent items quickly reach counts that make decay very unlikely, so they keep their buckets. Rare items keep replacing each other without affecting the frequent ones. An item that becomes frequent later in the stream can still outnumber a less frequent owner and take over its bucket.

Next to the table, the sketch keeps a min-heap with the k items that have the largest estimates so far. After an item's buckets are updated, if its estimate is larger than the smallest count in the heap, the item is added to the heap, and the smallest item is removed. If the item is already in the heap, its count is increased.

Unsure uses d = 2 rows of max(16k, 256) buckets, and a decay base of b = 0.8. The probabilities b^count are precomputed as 64-bit thresholds, so decay is cheap: the count c decreases if a random number is below the c-th threshold.

The original HeavyKeeper uses b = 1.08⁻¹ ≈ 0.93, and more rows. A smaller b lets frequent items lock their buckets faster, which makes the sketch more precise on flat streams. However, if b is too small (like 0.5), the first items to claim buckets keep them permanently, so items that become frequent later are never counted, even if they end up being the most frequent. Using b = 0.8 keeps most of the precision and still catches most late-arriving frequent items. As for the rows, two are enough to protect frequent items from collisions in a single row, and adding more rows only makes the sketch slower.

The item is hashed once. The hash is mapped to a position in each row by salting it (multiplying by a random per-row constant). The fingerprint is the top 32 bits of the hash. The heap uses the 64-bit hash to identify items, so it doesn't compare the actual item bytes.

Each bucket is 8 bytes (a 32-bit fingerprint and a 32-bit count), so the table takes 256·k bytes. The heap takes about 100 bytes per item plus the item itself.

The sketch uses wyhash for hashing and wyrand for random numbers.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks20, comparing unsure to keiler21 (HeavyKeeper with b = 0.9 and d = ln k) and dgryski22 (Filtered Space-Saving23) on the Zipf s=0.8 stream (time/op, lower is better):

Precision is the fraction of the reported top k that is in the true top k (higher is better):

Count error is the mean of |estimate − true| / true over the reported items (lower is better):

Unsure is 2–4× faster than the others for Add and 1.8–4× faster for Top. On flat streams (s=0.6), it finds the true top k with 90–97% precision, while keiler drops to 38–70% precision with a count error of 62–94%, and dgryski to 19–52% with counts 18× or more too high. On skewed streams (s=1.0), all three are about equally accurate.

HeavyKeeper: An Accurate Algorithm for Finding Top-k Elephant Flows by Junzhi Gong et al., 2018. ↩︎

Efficient Computation of Frequent and Top-k Elements in Data Streams by Ahmed Metwally et al., 2005. ↩︎

As engineers, we usually want exact answers from our data. But sometimes, allowing a bit of uncertainty can cut memory usage by tens, hundreds, or even thousands of times. That's where probabilistic data structures come in:

To use them in Go, try the nalgeon/unsure package:

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

Baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. #9911. Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests

New report calls for change, highlights hodgepodge governance and misunderstanding about tech’s limitations among officers

UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used.

According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing.

The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation.

It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards.

Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence.

In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken.

"We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.

"Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent."

Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning."

Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system.

However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries.

The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted.

The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes.

Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high.

Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute, as well as the King's College London Policy Institute, showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively.

Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience.

The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition.

Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns.

"Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said.

"A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence."

As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK.

Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made.

Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped.

The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements.

A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming.

Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals.

"The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said.

"This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited, as we've seen before.

"Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused."

Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®

#9909. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

The same snippet runs unchanged on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm) and Intel (XPU) GPUs, device_map="auto" places the model on whichever accelerator is available.

After loading the model, you can do text-only inference with it as follows.

We would need torchvision to be able to use images and text.

Muse Glimmer accepts images as input, as demonstrated here:

To work with videos we recommend installing torchcodec into the environment.

Muse Glimmer can answer complex questions about videos without audio. You can do video inference as follows, here’s an example from VideoMME2, which is the most popular video question answering benchmark.

Muse Glimmer can do multimodal tool calling, here’s how you can do it. In the example below, we ask the model to call the weather tool based on the city in the image.

You can use Muse Glimmer to do open ended object detection in images as follows.

Here is an end to end script to perform object detection GitHub Gist

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 llama.cpp support. Meta has distributed calibrated quants in this repo, and Unsloth is releasing optimized quants as well. DFlash speculative decoding is supported as well. You can use a pre-built llama binary to start a llama server or a CLI. To install llama.cpp, run:

Then you can start the server as follows.

Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:8080 to chat with the built-in WebUI.

You can also query the server as follows.

You can also use llama server with coding agents like Pi.

DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion drafter model to provide same output with extra speed-ups in decoding phase. Transformers and llama.cpp ship support for DFlash drafter of Muse Glimmer day-0.

Below you can see how speculative decoding can speed-up generation in realistic setups. The video shows llama.cpp webui with DFlash on the left and regular generation on the right.

You can load the drafter and model as follows, and infer like how you would with base model with an additional parameter (shown in the upcoming snippets).

You can start llama server using following command. --spec-draft-n-max argument controls how many future tokens DFlash proposes during each speculative-decoding step. Muse Glimmer’s DFlash model was trained with a block size of 16, one anchor token plus 15 proposed tokens, so any value above 15 will be clamped to 15.

You can also use llama cli with speculative decoding drafter as follows.

For a managed, autoscaling deployment, open the Muse Glimmer 30B Inference Endpoints preset. The model is already selected: choose the organization, cloud provider, region, compatible GPU instance, authentication, and autoscaling settings, then review the hourly price and click Create Endpoint. Once its status is Running, you can test it in the Playground and copy the endpoint URL and model name from the Overview.

The deployed model exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. Keep your Hugging Face token in an environment variable, set HF_ENDPOINT_URL to the URL shown in the Overview without /v1, and set HF_ENDPOINT_MODEL to the endpoint's model name.

See the Inference Endpoints documentation for configuration, autoscaling, security, logs, and monitoring.

For this release, we ship support for vLLM with transformers backend.

You can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

As part of this release, we ship an example to fine-tune Muse Glimmer on small split of MolmoWeb dataset. This shows how to make model generate structured outputs and how to fine-tune on images.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Let’s go team local 🚀

Assume the Inference Endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible /v1 API.

Set HF_TOKEN in the OpenClaw gateway environment, then add this to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Use the exact model ID returned by the endpoint’s /v1/models response if it differs.

If we hook up Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face MCP and update its AGENTS.md we give it the capability to find a quantized version of itself on the hub and run locally. This is handy if you want to work on something private, or just cut costs.

If you do this a second time, Muse Glimmer will find the cached weights and switch to them, so feel free to add a convenient command like /spawn.

Muse Glimmer inspects the machine and Hub, selects or creates a Q4_K_M GGUF, launches llama-server, and validates model discovery and chat completion. The result is a smaller local build behind an OpenAI-compatible API. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md.

https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/Muse%20Glimmer%20Quantisation%20Demo%20-%20explained.mp4?download=true

By adding this to AGENTS.md openclaw or hermes will be able to solve the rest.

Muse Glimmer can also take care of the opposite. Let’s get Glimmer to deploy itself on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints. Which is useful if you want to speed up on some cutting edge hardware.

N.B. You can also just deploy Muse Glimmer to Inference Endpoints directly and connect your agent.

Muse Glimmer pins the model revision, deploys it to a protected Hugging Face Inference Endpoint, and verifies health, model discovery, and chat completion. It then connects the Claw agent with secrets and rollback preserved. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer will also need the Hugging Face MCP and/or the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

Finally, let’s get Muse Glimmer to do some light RSI. We can instruct our agent to optimize its own inference engine for specific hardware, in this case a Nvidia H100. To do this, the agent will need to use another inference engine, like Inference Endpoints above.

Muse Glimmer benchmarks its own single-H100 serving stack, testing one reversible change at a time while holding the workload fixed. It keeps only correctness-passing gains and finishes with the fastest reproducible configuration. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer need the Hugging Face MCP and the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/onyx-optimization-progress.gif?download=true

Try Muse Glimmer as a Hugging Face research agent. The Gradio Space sends each model request to a private Hugging Face Inference Endpoint through its OpenAI-compatible API. It also connects to the official Hugging Face MCP server, giving the agent read-only tools to search and inspect Hub repositories, models, datasets, Spaces, documentation, and papers.

We are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a New Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏

#9908. Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year

Watchdog wants assurances from 200 execs that employees aren't poking around patient files they have no business viewing

The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it.

The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment.

ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see.

"Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said.

In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping.

Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't.

Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order.

The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news.

This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison.

That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't.

Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed.

The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025.

And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018.

Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch.

"I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said.

With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

#9907. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

#9906. A NES emulator written in Odin

I’ve started this project in late June of 2024. I’ve worked on it in my spare time off and on. I decided to put a pause on this project in January 2025 to focus on other things.

It’s been a wild ride. I’ve had a lot of fun, but I’ve also suffered more towards the end, when trying to make the emulator “fully” accurate.

You can read the Github Readme for more info about the project.

I’ve seen some people say that making a NES emulator is a simple weekend project, and I frankly found that baffling. Because evidently, it’s not. It took me 7 months to get my emulator to how it is now.

I think what they actually mean is that getting a NES emulator “working” takes a short time. Like maybe getting Donkey Kong to run. And that’s true. You can get to 80% or maybe 90% pretty fast. It’s the last 10% that takes a long, long time.

The NES hardware has many idiosyncrasies that need to be emulated for certain games to run. Many games depend on very specific NES behavior. And if you don’t implement it right, they won’t run. A lot of the challenge is about timing. The CPU and the PPU (the chip that handles the graphics rendering in the NES) run in parallel and they communicate with each other. That timing needs to be very accurate, or many wrong things can happen. Most games will run fine with a less than accurate emulator, but a lot of them won’t, and they will need you to consider things in more detail.

Another issue is mappers. Mappers are what we call an implementation of a type of cartridge. You see, NES games come in cartridges, and cartridges aren’t just data. They are circuitry with their own behavior and extra resources like read-only memory, and writable memory. Some come with extra audio capabilities, but I haven’t implemented that.

Anyway, you have to implement these mappers if you want a game that comes in that cartridge to run in your game. They complete the NES’s circuitry. In a way, they are a part of the NES hardware. There are many mappers, but you can support a lot of games by just implementing a few. I’ve had trouble implementing some mappers, and some of them are still badly implemented, causing some games to not work. I found it hard to understand some of the mapper documentation.

The biggest challenge with making an emulator, I think, is to know what to implement. Information about the hardware, and what needs to be emulated about the hardware for games to work in your emulator. Thankfully, the NES is very well documented online. I’ve used many resources, like:

I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without these resources and the help from people in the nesdev discord.

I’ve learned a lot about Odin while making this project. I think it fit this project like a glove. Being a very simple, strongly typed C-like language that gives me all the freedom I want makes making an emulator much easier than using other languages, I feel.

One thing that threw me off was that Odin has no automatic integer promotion. When doing calculations on numbers, Odin will never promote types to a bigger one. That led to a few bugs. But I blame this all on me and me being used to C’s integer promotion.

One fun thing that I’ve learned was doing a bit of memory allocation strategy. Odin has no automatic memory management, so you have to come up with smart ways to handle memory. I’ve had fun thinking about how I should handle memory best. I didn’t need to do anything complicated. I mostly use one temporary allocator that clears every frame, a global heap allocator for things that need to live forever, and a NES Arena allocator for anything that needs to live along a NES session. I found memory allocation fun.

Another thing I had to learn is how to serialize Odin objects. I used the CBOR library, and I ran into a few issues. I thought my code was misbehaving due to a bug in the library, but that was cleared up. It was only having trouble because I made a few odd types that it didn’t know how to serialize. Once I learned how to properly write custom handling for types, everything worked perfectly. This was one of the tricky types that cbor didn’t know how to serialize:

I love how Odin lets you define raw unions like this, and with bit fields. It fits emulator development very well.

I don’t consider this project “finished”. Of course, a project like this is never truly finished, but a lot of aspects of it need a lot of work, for sure:

These are the main things that are lacking at this moment. Maybe at some point I will return and keep working on this so the project can feel “complete”.

#9905. BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn

The Boss mentions 'AI security,' triggering an entirely proportionate incident response

Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach...

And look, the Boss has his office door open!

The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open.

His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us.

And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas.

"AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop.

He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town.

"For the security system," the Boss teases.

I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same.

The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea.

"Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed."

"And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too."

"It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to.

"I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing.

So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him.

Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow...

On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously.

The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight.

On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling.

"Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback.

"It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!"

Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard.

"It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!"

"I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks.

Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device...

The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan.

"So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden.

"Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor."

"It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation."

"It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used."

"Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know."

"Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks.

"Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie.

"So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building."

"And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad."

"Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious.
